description: Go language intricacies (types, errors, generics, concurrency, memory, tooling) and the Go side of Kubernetes operators: client-go, apimachinery, controller-runtime, Kubebuilder, testing and observability. For a platform architect who reads and writes Go controllers.

notes.front: In Go, what does a newly declared struct contain, and what API-design idiom follows from it?
notes.back: Every field holds its type's zero value (0, "", nil, false). Idiom: make the zero value usable without a constructor, e.g. sync.Mutex{}, bytes.Buffer{}.
notes.analogy: Like a new phone that works out of the box on factory defaults, no setup wizard required.

notes.front: How does a Go type come to satisfy an interface?
notes.back: Implicitly and structurally: if its method set contains every method of the interface. There is no implements keyword, and the check happens at compile time.
notes.analogy: A job ad listing skills: anyone who has the skills qualifies, without ever applying to that ad by name.
notes.extra: Contrast: like duck typing, but verified by the compiler (closer to TypeScript's structural typing).

notes.front: In Go, is a pointer-receiver method in the method set of T, *T, or both?
notes.back: Only *T. Value-receiver methods are in both. So if an interface method has a pointer receiver, only &v satisfies the interface, not v.

notes.front: A type T defines func (t *T) String() string. What does fmt.Println(v) print for a value v of type T, and why?
notes.back: The default struct formatting, not your String(). The method belongs only to *T's method set, so a T value does not satisfy fmt.Stringer; fmt.Println(&v) would call it.

notes.front: Why can err != nil be true when a function returned a nil *MyError as error?
notes.back: An interface value is a (type, value) pair. A nil *MyError stored in it has its type set, so the interface itself is non-nil.
notes.analogy: A labelled but empty box is still a box: only having no box at all counts as nil.
notes.extra: Fix: return a literal nil on success, never a typed nil pointer variable (var e *MyErr; return e).

notes.front: How do you avoid the typed-nil error bug?
notes.back: Return a literal nil for the error result on success. Never declare var e *MyError and return it as error, because that wraps a nil pointer in a non-nil interface.

notes.front: What does using any (e.g. map[string]any for API payloads) cost compared with a defined struct?
notes.back: Compile-time type safety: every read needs a runtime type assertion and field-name typos go unnoticed. A struct with json tags serialises the same way, statically checked.

notes.front: Go array vs slice: what is the difference?
notes.back: Array: fixed length that is part of the type ([4]int), copied by value. Slice: a header {pointer, len, cap} over a backing array, grown with append.
notes.analogy: A slice is a bookmark with a length into a bookshelf (the array); several bookmarks can point into the same shelf.

notes.front: Go has no inheritance. What does struct embedding do instead, and what can it NOT do that inheritance can?
notes.back: It promotes the inner type's fields and methods onto the outer type (composition). No subtyping or virtual dispatch: the embedded type never calls the outer type's overrides, and a same-named outer method only shadows the promoted one.
notes.analogy: A shop that houses a post-office counter: customers can use the counter through the shop, but the counter doesn't know it's inside a shop.

notes.front: What is the API risk of embedding a struct just to reuse its methods?
notes.back: Every exported method of the embedded type is promoted into the outer type's public API, widening and coupling it beyond what was intended.

notes.front: Why is an embedded (unnamed) sync.Mutex in an exported struct usually a mistake?
notes.back: Lock()/Unlock() are promoted into the type's public API, so callers can lock it directly. Use a named unexported field: mu sync.Mutex.

notes.front: Go byte vs rune?
notes.back: byte = uint8, one raw byte. rune = int32, one Unicode code point, which may take several bytes in UTF-8.
notes.extra: len(s) counts bytes; for i, r := range s iterates runes.

notes.front: What does iota do inside a Go const block?
notes.back: An untyped counter that starts at 0 in each const block and increments per line; used to build enumerated constants.

notes.front: Why can't you modify a Go string in place?
notes.back: A string is a read-only {pointer, length} header over bytes. To change it, convert to []byte (a copy), mutate, and convert back.

notes.front: When does == on two Go struct values compile?
notes.back: Only if every field is comparable. Structs containing slices, maps or funcs cannot be compared with == (compile error); comparison is field by field.

notes.front: What does the two-value type assertion v, ok := x.(T) give you that v := x.(T) does not?
notes.back: No panic on mismatch: ok is false and v is T's zero value, so an unexpected dynamic type can be handled.

notes.front: Why does Go favour small, single-method interfaces like io.Reader?
notes.back: They are trivial to implement and compose (io.ReadWriter), so many types satisfy them and code accepting them works with files, sockets and buffers alike.

notes.front: What does the Go idiom "accept interfaces, return structs" mean, and why?
notes.back: Take the narrowest interface you need as a parameter (flexible for callers); return concrete types so callers keep the full API and can define their own narrow interfaces.

notes.front: Where should a Go interface be declared, and what is "interface pollution"?
notes.back: At the consumer (point of use), not beside the implementation. Pollution: declaring interfaces before a second implementation or real need exists, adding indirection for nothing.

notes.front: In Go, what is the method set of an interface that embeds other interfaces?
notes.back: The union of the embedded interfaces' methods plus its own, e.g. io.ReadWriter = io.Reader + io.Writer.

notes.front: What is fmt.Stringer and when is it called automatically?
notes.back: String() string. fmt calls it when printing the value with %v/%s (and Print/Println).

notes.front: How do you make the compiler verify that *MyType implements MyInterface?
notes.back: var _ MyInterface = (*MyType)(nil): a blank-identifier assignment that fails to compile if the method set is incomplete, at zero runtime cost.

notes.front: What is Go's error type?
notes.back: A built-in interface: type error interface { Error() string }. Any type with that method is an error.

notes.front: What is a sentinel error, and how should callers test for it?
notes.back: A package-level error value (var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")). Test with errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound), which walks the wrap chain; == misses wrapped errors.

notes.front: errors.Is vs errors.As?
notes.back:
Is: does the chain contain this value (a sentinel)?
As: does it contain an error of this type? If so, assign it to the target pointer.

notes.front: How do you extract a *fs.PathError from a possibly wrapped error?
notes.back:
var pe *fs.PathError
if errors.As(err, &pe) { log(pe.Path) }

notes.front: How do you add context to an error while keeping the original inspectable?
notes.back: fmt.Errorf("reading config: %w", err). %w wraps (reachable via Unwrap/Is/As); %v would flatten it into plain text.
notes.analogy: %w puts the original error inside a labelled envelope; %v photocopies its text onto a new page and the original is gone.

notes.front: Why not check Go errors by comparing err.Error() strings?
notes.back: Message text is not part of the API contract and changes between versions. Sentinels or typed errors with errors.Is/As are the stable contract.

notes.front: When is panic idiomatic in Go, versus returning an error?
notes.back: Only for programmer bugs and broken invariants. Expected failures (bad input, missing file) return errors, above all in libraries, which must not force callers to recover.
notes.analogy: panic is pulling the emergency brake; returning an error is the conductor announcing a delay.

notes.front: What does recover() do, and where must it be called to work?
notes.back: Stops a panic and returns its value, but only when called directly inside a deferred function in the panicking goroutine.
notes.analogy: recover is a safety net that only works if it is strung up (deferred) under the same trapeze (goroutine) before the fall.

notes.front: Can recover catch a panic raised in another goroutine?
notes.back: No. An unrecovered panic in any goroutine crashes the whole program, so each goroutine that may panic needs its own deferred recover.
notes.extra: In practice: HTTP servers recover per request goroutine; your own go func() does not inherit that.

notes.front: What is errors.Join (Go 1.20+) for?
notes.back: Combining several errors into one that still matches errors.Is/As for each, e.g. aggregating failures from concurrent work.

notes.front: Why is _ = someFunc() discarding an error a serious smell in Go?
notes.back: Errors are values, not exceptions: the return value is the only failure signal. Dropping it turns a detectable failure into silent bad state downstream. errcheck-style linters flag it.

notes.front: Where should you wrap errors with context, and where not?
notes.back: Wrap at boundaries (I/O, network, package edges) where knowledge of which call/resource failed is about to be lost. Don't re-wrap at every frame of one logical call: it just adds noise.

notes.front: In func Map[T, U any](s []T, f func(T) U) []U, what are T and U?
notes.back: Type parameters, declared in square brackets and constrained here by any; the compiler instantiates them per call.

notes.front: What is a type constraint in Go generics?
notes.back: An interface stating which types (or methods/operators) a type parameter accepts, e.g. cmp.Ordered for types supporting <.

notes.front: What does ~int mean in a Go constraint?
notes.back: Any type whose underlying type is int, so type Age int qualifies, not just int itself.

notes.front: Can a Go method declare its own type parameters?
notes.back: No. Methods may use the receiver type's parameters but cannot add new ones; only top-level functions can.

notes.front: What is the built-in comparable constraint for?
notes.back: Types supporting ==/!=; needed for generic map keys and sets.

notes.front: When can a Go generic call omit explicit type arguments?
notes.back: When they can be inferred from the ordinary arguments (Map(ints, double) infers T). Explicit [T] is needed only when inference is impossible or ambiguous.

notes.front: When should you reach for generics rather than a small interface?
notes.back: For type-independent containers and algorithms (sets, Map/Filter helpers). If behaviour varies by type, a small interface is usually cleaner.

notes.front: Why can Go generic code be slower than hand-specialised code, unlike C++ templates?
notes.back: Go uses partial monomorphisation ("GC shape stenciling" plus dictionaries), not full per-type code generation, so some calls go through indirection, especially with interface-heavy constraints.

notes.front: How do you declare a generic Stack type and its Push method in Go?
notes.back:
type Stack[T any] struct { items []T }
func (s *Stack[T]) Push(v T)

notes.front: What do the slices and maps standard packages (Go 1.21+) provide?
notes.back: Generic helpers over slices and maps (Contains, Sort, Equal, Clone, DeleteFunc...), replacing hand-rolled loops.

notes.front: What is a goroutine, and why can you run thousands of them?
notes.back: A function running concurrently, scheduled by the Go runtime onto OS threads (M:N). It starts with a small stack (a few KB) that grows on demand, so it is cheap.
notes.analogy: Many order tickets, few cooks: the cooks (OS threads) work through tickets and set aside any order that is waiting on the oven.

notes.front: What is a goroutine leak?
notes.back: A goroutine that stays blocked (typically on a channel op that never completes) after it is no longer needed, so its stack and everything it references are never freed.
notes.analogy: A worker still waiting at a pickup counter that closed for good: never sent home, still on the payroll.

notes.front: A function starts a goroutine that sends its result on an unbuffered channel, then returns early on an error without receiving. What breaks, and what are two fixes?
notes.back: The goroutine blocks on the send forever (a leak). Fixes: give the channel a buffer of 1 so the send always completes, or select on ctx.Done() in the goroutine.

notes.front: What rule prevents most goroutine leaks?
notes.back: Decide at creation how the goroutine stops (context cancellation, channel close, WaitGroup). Never fire-and-forget.

notes.front: Before Go 1.22, what went wrong with for _, v := range xs { go func() { use(v) }() }?
notes.back: All closures shared one loop variable, so goroutines often saw the last value. Collecting &v had the same bug: every pointer was the same address.

notes.front: What did Go 1.22 change about loop variables, and when does the change apply?
notes.back: Each iteration gets a fresh variable, fixing closure and &v capture. It applies only to modules whose go.mod declares go 1.22 or later.

notes.front: How is sync.WaitGroup used?
notes.back: Add(n) before launching, each goroutine calls Done() (usually deferred), and the caller's Wait() blocks until the counter reaches zero.
notes.analogy: A tour guide counting heads: add to the count before people leave the bus, each says "done" on return, the guide waits for zero.

notes.front: Why must wg.Add() be called before go f(), not inside the goroutine?
notes.back: Otherwise Wait() may run first, see a zero counter and return before the goroutine has registered: a race.

notes.front: What does GOMAXPROCS control?
notes.back: The maximum number of OS threads executing Go code at once (parallelism). Defaults to the number of usable CPUs.
notes.extra: K8s: before Go 1.25 the default ignored container CPU limits (hence uber-go/automaxprocs); Go 1.25+ honours cgroup CPU limits.

notes.front: Why doesn't running far more goroutines than GOMAXPROCS hurt I/O-bound throughput?
notes.back: Goroutines blocked on I/O or channels are parked and use no CPU; the scheduler runs other runnable goroutines on the free threads.

notes.front: What is the danger of spawning one goroutine per request with no limit?
notes.back: Under load, memory and scheduler work grow faster than work completes. Bound concurrency with a worker pool or a semaphore.

notes.front: What is the worker-pool pattern in Go?
notes.back: A fixed N goroutines read jobs from a shared channel and write to a results channel, bounding concurrency to N regardless of job count.

notes.front: What does runtime.Gosched() do, and why is it rarely needed?
notes.back: Yields the processor to other runnable goroutines without blocking. Rarely needed because the scheduler has been preemptive since Go 1.14.

notes.front: Unbuffered vs buffered Go channel?
notes.back: Unbuffered: a send blocks until a receiver takes it (synchronous hand-off). Buffered: a send blocks only when the buffer is full.
notes.analogy: Unbuffered is handing over a baton hand to hand; buffered is a mailbox with N slots.

notes.front: What happens on a send or receive on a nil channel?
notes.back: It blocks forever. Used on purpose to disable a select case by setting its channel to nil.
notes.analogy: A phone line that was never connected: dial it and you wait forever.

notes.front: What happens when you send on a closed channel?
notes.back: A panic. Only the sender closes a channel, and only once.

notes.front: To stop many goroutines at once, why close(done) rather than sending a value on done?
notes.back: A send wakes exactly one receiver. A close is observed by every receiver, now and in the future, so it works as a broadcast.

notes.front: What happens when you receive from a closed channel?
notes.back: Buffered values are still delivered first; then each receive returns immediately with the zero value and ok == false.

notes.front: What is the channel-ownership idiom?
notes.back: One goroutine (usually the creator) owns the channel: it alone sends and closes. Receivers never close, which avoids send-on-closed and double-close panics.
notes.analogy: Only the host locks up at closing time; guests never lock the door behind them.

notes.front: Why must a producer close(ch) rather than just stop sending?
notes.back: Closing tells receivers "no more values": for range ch ends and ok becomes false. Without it, consumers block forever, a common leak.

notes.front: What does a default case do in a Go select?
notes.back: Makes the select non-blocking: if no case is ready right now, default runs.

notes.front: What are fan-out and fan-in in Go concurrency?
notes.back: Fan-out: several workers read from one input channel. Fan-in: several result channels are merged into one for the consumer.

notes.front: What is a Go pipeline?
notes.back: Stages connected by channels, each a goroutine that receives, transforms and sends on. Small or unbuffered channels give natural back-pressure.
notes.analogy: An assembly line with short conveyors between stations: when a conveyor is full, the upstream station waits.

notes.front: How do you make pipeline stages stop cleanly when downstream quits early?
notes.back: Every send and receive selects on both the data channel and ctx.Done() (or a done channel), so a stage can exit instead of blocking forever.

notes.front: "Share memory by communicating": when is a mutex still the better choice in Go?
notes.back: For simple shared state (a counter, a cache map), a mutex is clearer and faster. Channels shine for hand-offs, pipelines and signalling; Go doesn't require them everywhere.

notes.front: sync.Mutex vs sync.RWMutex?
notes.back: Mutex: one holder at a time. RWMutex: many concurrent readers (RLock) or one writer (Lock); helps only read-heavy workloads.
notes.analogy: A museum gallery: many visitors may look at once, but the curator rehanging pictures needs the room empty.

notes.front: What does sync.Once guarantee?
notes.back: once.Do(f) runs f exactly once even with concurrent callers, and all callers return after it has finished; used for lazy initialisation.

notes.front: What breaks if you pass a struct containing a sync.Mutex by value?
notes.back: The copy gets its own independent lock state, so goroutines using different copies no longer exclude each other. go vet (copylocks) flags it; pass a pointer instead.

notes.front: When is sync/atomic preferable to a mutex?
notes.back: For a single counter or flag: lock-free Add/Load/Store/CompareAndSwap are cheaper. It can't keep several related fields consistent; that needs a mutex.

notes.front: What does go test -race detect, and what is its blind spot?
notes.back: Unsynchronised concurrent accesses (at least one a write) to the same memory, caught at runtime. It only sees races that actually happen on the executed paths.
notes.analogy: A speed camera: it only catches the drivers who speed past while it is switched on.

notes.front: In the Go memory model, what does a happens-before edge guarantee?
notes.back: That writes before it are visible to the other goroutine after it, e.g. a channel send happens-before the matching receive completes; Unlock before the next Lock. Without such an edge, a reader may see stale values.

notes.front: What three things does context.Context carry down a call chain?
notes.back: Cancellation, deadlines/timeouts, and request-scoped values. By convention it is the first parameter, named ctx.

notes.front: How does a goroutine notice that its context was cancelled?
notes.back: It selects on ctx.Done(), a channel closed on cancel or expiry, then reads ctx.Err() (Canceled or DeadlineExceeded).
notes.analogy: Done() is a fire alarm everyone downstream can hear: nobody polls a shared flag; the bell rings and each goroutine leaves.

notes.text: Context constructors: WithCancel gives {{c1::a manual cancel function}}; WithTimeout cancels {{c2::after a duration}}; WithDeadline cancels {{c3::at a fixed point in time}}.

notes.front: Why call a context's cancel even if the timeout will fire anyway?
notes.back: It frees the timer and the parent-child link immediately; otherwise they live until expiry. Idiom: defer cancel() right after creating it. go vet flags a lost cancel.

notes.front: Why is passing business parameters via context.WithValue an anti-pattern?
notes.back: It hides data flow and loses type safety (untyped keys, runtime assertions). Reserve it for cross-cutting request metadata such as trace IDs or auth info.

notes.front: context.Background() vs context.TODO()?
notes.back: Both are empty, never-cancelled roots. Background: deliberate top level (main, tests). TODO: placeholder where a real context should be plumbed in later.

notes.front: When a parent context is cancelled, what happens to contexts derived from it, and what happens when a child is cancelled?
notes.back: Cancelling a parent cancels all descendants. Cancelling a child affects only that child and its own descendants, never the parent.

notes.front: What does errgroup (golang.org/x/sync) add over sync.WaitGroup?
notes.back: Wait() returns the first error from the group, and errgroup.WithContext cancels a shared context when any goroutine fails, so siblings stop early. SetLimit bounds concurrency.

notes.front: What is escape analysis in Go, and why does it matter?
notes.back: Compile-time analysis of whether a value can outlive its function. If not it stays on the stack; if it might, it escapes to the heap, which costs an allocation and GC work.
notes.analogy: The stack is a desk cleared when you leave the meeting; the heap is a shared storeroom someone (the GC) must tidy later.

notes.front: Name two common reasons a Go value escapes to the heap.
notes.back: Returning a pointer to a local, and storing it in an interface (e.g. passing it to fmt.Println or an any parameter).

notes.front: Slice length vs capacity?
notes.back: Length: elements currently accessible. Capacity: room in the backing array from the slice's start; append uses it without reallocating.

notes.front: When does append reallocate, and why must you always use its result?
notes.back: Only when capacity is insufficient; otherwise it writes into the same backing array. Because the returned header may point to new memory, always write s = append(s, x).

notes.front: Why can sub-slicing (b := a[:2]) cause aliasing bugs?
notes.back: b shares a's backing array: writes through one show in the other, and append(b, x) can overwrite a[2] while capacity remains.
notes.analogy: Two windows onto the same room: rearrange furniture through one and the other sees it too.
notes.extra: Fix: full slice expression a[:2:2] caps capacity so append copies; or slices.Clone.

notes.front: How does Go's garbage collector work, at a high level?
notes.back: Concurrent tri-colour mark-and-sweep running alongside the program with short stop-the-world phases; tuned for low pause times rather than maximum throughput.
notes.extra: Knobs: GOGC (heap growth ratio) and GOMEMLIMIT (Go 1.19+; set near the container memory limit to avoid OOM kills).

notes.front: Passing structs by value vs pointer in Go: what is the trade-off?
notes.back: Values copy every field but stay on the stack and can't be aliased; pointers avoid the copy but may escape to the heap and allow shared mutation. Small structs by value, large or mutable ones by pointer.

notes.front: Why can passing a large array (not slice) to a Go function be costly?
notes.back: Arrays are values: the whole array is copied. A slice passes only its 3-word header. The syntax looks similar, so it happens by accident.

notes.front: Why is s += x in a loop slow in Go, and what's the fix?
notes.back: Strings are immutable, so each += allocates and copies: O(n²) overall. Use strings.Builder (or bytes.Buffer).

notes.front: What does defer cost?
notes.back: Very little since Go 1.14's open-coded defers; it only matters in extremely hot, tight loops.

notes.text: A nil map in Go: reading returns {{c1::the value type's zero value (no panic)}}; writing {{c2::panics ("assignment to entry in nil map")}}.
notes.extra: Initialise with make or a literal. A nil slice, by contrast, is fine for len, range and append.

notes.front: Why is defer f.Close() inside a loop usually a bug?
notes.back: Deferred calls run when the function returns, not per iteration, so every file stays open until then and descriptors can run out. Move the body into a helper function or close explicitly.
notes.analogy: Stacking every dish to wash after the whole party instead of after each course: the cupboard runs out first.

notes.front: Why compare time.Time values with Equal() instead of ==?
notes.back: == also compares the monotonic reading and the location, which differ for the same instant (e.g. after serialisation). Equal compares the instant only.

notes.front: What happens if two goroutines write to the same Go map at once, and how do you prevent it?
notes.back: The runtime usually detects it and aborts with an unrecoverable fatal error (concurrent map writes); recover cannot catch it. Guard the map with a mutex, or use sync.Map for suitable access patterns.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: Why does a lowercase struct field never appear in encoding/json output?
notes.back: Unexported fields are invisible to reflection-based packages, so they are silently skipped when marshalling and unmarshalling.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: How does encoding/json handle an embedded anonymous struct?
notes.back: Its exported fields are promoted and flattened into the parent JSON object (unless the embedded field has a json tag name).

notes.front: What is the classic := shadowing bug with err?
notes.back: Inside an inner block, x, err := f() declares a new err, so the outer err is never set and the failure is lost. go vet -vettool=shadow and linters catch it.

notes.front: Why was time.After inside a for { select { ... } } loop a known leak?
notes.back: Before Go 1.23 each call created a timer that was not collected until it fired, so hot loops piled up timers. Go 1.23+ collects unreferenced timers, but reusing one time.NewTimer with Reset is still cheaper.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: What are the single methods of io.Reader and io.Writer?
notes.back: Read(p []byte) (n int, err error) and Write(p []byte) (n int, err error): the base of nearly all Go I/O.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: Why must an io.Reader caller process n bytes before checking err?
notes.back: A Read may return n > 0 and a non-nil error in the same call (e.g. final data plus io.EOF). Checking err first drops that data.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: What is table-driven testing in Go?
notes.back: One test function loops over a slice of cases (name, input, want) and runs the same assertions on each. Adding a case is a one-line change.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: What does t.Run(name, func) give you in Go tests?
notes.back: Named subtests that pass, fail and skip independently and can be selected with -run 'TestX/case'; also allow t.Parallel() per case.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: What does t.Helper() do?
notes.back: Marks a test helper so failures are reported at the caller's line rather than inside the helper.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: t.Error vs t.Fatal?
notes.back: Error: mark failed and continue. Fatal: mark failed and stop the test goroutine immediately (must be called from the test goroutine).

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: Why is reflect a last resort in Go?
notes.back: It is slow, bypasses compile-time type checking and hurts readability. It's justified for generic infrastructure such as encoding/json.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: What does the struct tag json:"name,omitempty" do?
notes.back: Read via reflection by encoding/json: the field is serialised as name, and omitted when it holds its zero value.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: What is net/http's Handler interface?
notes.back: ServeHTTP(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request): the one method every handler, middleware and router builds on.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: How is HTTP middleware written in standard-library Go?
notes.back: A function that takes an http.Handler and returns a new one wrapping it: func Logging(next http.Handler) http.Handler; compose by nesting.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: Why do kubectl-style CLIs use cobra instead of the standard flag package?
notes.back: flag parses flags into variables but has no subcommand support (tool get pods), help trees or completion.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: What does go.mod declare, and why does its go directive matter?
notes.back: Module path, required dependency versions, and the language version the code assumes. The go line switches semantics, e.g. per-iteration loop variables from 1.22.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: What is Minimal Version Selection (MVS) in Go modules?
notes.back: For each dependency Go picks the minimum version that satisfies every requirement in the graph, not the newest available, so builds are reproducible without a lock file.
notes.analogy: The meeting time is the latest of everyone's "earliest I can make it", not "whenever is newest".

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: What is go.sum for?
notes.back: Cryptographic hashes of every module version used, checked on download to detect tampering or changed content (backed by the checksum database).
notes.analogy: A tamper-evident seal on every package you install.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: Why must a Go module's import path change for v2+?
notes.back: Semantic import versioning: a path implies backward compatibility, so a breaking major version gets a new path (.../v2). v1 and v2 can then coexist in one build.
notes.analogy: A new edition of a book gets a new ISBN, so both editions can sit on the same shelf.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: What is a //go:build constraint used for?
notes.back: Including a file only for matching OS, architecture or custom tags, e.g. platform-specific code or //go:build integration tests.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: What does go vet catch that the compiler doesn't?
notes.back: Suspicious but legal code: Printf format/argument mismatches, copied locks, malformed struct tags, unreachable code, lost context cancels.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: Does go build run //go:generate commands? Why does that matter for generated code (stringer, mockgen, controller-gen)?
notes.back: No. go generate runs only when invoked explicitly, so you must rerun it after changing inputs and commit the generated files.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: What problem does a go.work workspace solve?
notes.back: Developing several local modules together (a library and its consumer) without editing replace directives into each go.mod.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::07 Stdlib, Testing & Tooling
notes.front: go mod tidy vs go mod vendor?
notes.back: tidy: add missing and drop unused requirements in go.mod/go.sum based on imports. vendor: copy all dependency source into vendor/ for offline builds.
notes.extra: Why vendor: air-gapped, reproducible CI and protection against upstream removal; Kubernetes itself vendors.

notes.front: What is a client-go clientset?
notes.back: Generated, statically typed clients per API group and version for built-in kinds, e.g. cs.CoreV1().Pods(ns).Get(ctx, name, opts).

notes.front: When do you need client-go's dynamic client instead of a typed clientset?
notes.back: When the kind is unknown at compile time (CRDs without Go types, generic tooling). It works on unstructured.Unstructured, a map[string]any wrapper that implements runtime.Object.

notes.front: Why can a typed client lose data that an unstructured client keeps?
notes.back: Typed decoding drops JSON fields absent from the compiled Go struct (e.g. fields added in a newer API version). Unstructured keeps the full object, so an update doesn't erase them.

notes.front: What is a client-go Informer, and what problem does it solve?
notes.back: A watch-backed local cache of one resource type that fires add/update/delete handlers. Controllers read from memory instead of repeatedly LISTing the API server.
notes.analogy: A newspaper subscription with your own archive: you read your copy rather than phoning the newsroom for every question.

notes.front: What is the ListAndWatch pattern behind informers?
notes.back: LIST once to get the full state and its resourceVersion, then WATCH for changes from that version onward.

notes.front: What happens when a watch's resourceVersion is too old (410 Gone)?
notes.back: etcd has compacted that history, so changes can't be replayed. The client must re-LIST; informers do this automatically.
notes.analogy: Asking for "every issue since #100" after old issues were pulped: you buy today's complete edition (re-LIST) and continue from there.

notes.front: What does an informer's resync period actually do?
notes.back: Periodically re-delivers every object in the local cache to the update handlers, without calling the API server, so controllers re-reconcile and fix drift in external systems.

notes.front: Informer resync vs relist: what is the difference?
notes.back:
Resync: replays the local cache to handlers on a timer; no API traffic.
Relist: a fresh LIST from the API server after a watch error or expired resourceVersion.

notes.front: What is a client-go Lister?
notes.back: A read-only accessor that serves Get/List from an informer's local indexed store: fast, no API calls, eventually consistent.

notes.front: What does a SharedInformerFactory provide?
notes.back: One informer per resource type shared by every consumer in the process, so several controllers reuse a single watch and cache.

notes.front: What does a client-go workqueue add between event handlers and reconcile logic?
notes.back: Deduplication (many events for one key become one item), rate-limited retries with backoff, and a guarantee that one key isn't processed by two workers at once.
notes.analogy: A to-do list where writing the same task twice leaves one entry, and failed tasks come back with ever-longer snooze times.

notes.front: Why do client-go controllers enqueue namespace/name keys rather than objects?
notes.back: The object may change again before it's processed. Fetching by key from the cache at processing time acts on the latest state, and keys deduplicate in the queue.
notes.analogy: A kitchen ticket names the table, not a photo of the plate: the cook checks the table's current order when getting to it.

notes.front: What is cache.DeletedFinalStateUnknown in an informer delete handler?
notes.back: A tombstone delivered when the delete event itself was missed (seen only on relist). The handler must type-check for it and use its Key/Obj (possibly stale).

notes.front: What is client-go's discovery client used for?
notes.back: Asking a cluster at runtime which API groups, versions and resources it serves, since CRDs and API versions vary between clusters. Also feeds the RESTMapper (GVK to GVR).

notes.front: Why do controllers configure rest.Config.QPS and Burst?
notes.back: They set client-go's token-bucket rate limiter, so a controller processing many objects doesn't flood or get throttled by the API server.

notes.front: What is runtime.Object in apimachinery?
notes.back: The interface every API type implements (GetObjectKind(), DeepCopyObject()), letting clients, schemes and serializers handle any kind generically.

notes.front: What is an apimachinery Scheme?
notes.back: A registry mapping Go types to GroupVersionKinds and back, plus conversion and defaulting functions. Types must be registered (AddToScheme) before a client can serialise them.

notes.front: GroupVersionKind vs GroupVersionResource?
notes.back: GVK names a type as written in manifests (apps/v1, Kind=Deployment). GVR names the REST collection (apps/v1, deployments). A RESTMapper translates between them.
notes.analogy: GVK is the species name on a specimen label; GVR is the museum drawer where all specimens of that species are filed.

notes.front: Why does each Kubernetes API package have a generated zz_generated.deepcopy.go?
notes.back: runtime.Object requires DeepCopyObject() and Go has no built-in deep copy. Generated copies let caches hand out objects safely; mutating a cached object without copying corrupts the cache.
notes.analogy: Cached objects are library reference books: photocopy (DeepCopy) before scribbling on them.

notes.front: What does metav1.Object (via meta.Accessor) give generic controller code?
notes.back: Uniform access to ObjectMeta (name, namespace, labels, annotations, ownerReferences, resourceVersion) whatever the concrete kind.

notes.front: What does an apimachinery codec/serializer do?
notes.back: Encodes and decodes objects between Go structs and JSON, YAML or protobuf, using the Scheme to resolve kinds and versions.

notes.front: What do registered defaulting functions (SetDefaults_X) do?
notes.back: Fill unset fields with API-defined defaults when an object is decoded, so downstream code sees a fully populated object.

notes.front: What does controller-runtime's Manager own?
notes.back: The process-level pieces: shared cache and informers, the client, Scheme, leader election, metrics and health endpoints, and the lifecycle of every registered controller and webhook.
notes.analogy: The Manager is the stage manager: it owns the stage, lights and shared props, and cues each controller.
notes.extra: HA: set LeaderElection: true in Manager options; a Lease ensures only one replica runs the controllers.

notes.front: What goes wrong if you run two replicas of an operator without leader election?
notes.back: Both reconcile the same objects concurrently, causing conflicting writes and duplicate side effects. Leader election lets only one replica run the controllers while the others wait as hot standbys.

notes.front: What is the controller-runtime Reconciler interface?
notes.back: Reconcile(ctx, req ctrl.Request) (ctrl.Result, error). It gets only a namespace/name and must drive actual state toward desired state idempotently.

notes.front: controller-runtime's default Client vs mgr.GetAPIReader()?
notes.back: The default client reads from the shared informer cache (fast, eventually consistent) and writes to the API server. The APIReader reads straight from the API server when you need a guaranteed fresh read.
notes.analogy: The cached client reads your inbox snapshot; the APIReader phones the person directly.
notes.extra: Pitfall: a cached read can lag; conflict detection via resourceVersion on write is what keeps read-then-write safe.

notes.front: What does Builder.For(&MyType{}) set up?
notes.back: The primary resource: any change to a MyType object enqueues a reconcile for that object.

notes.front: What does Builder.Owns(&appsv1.Deployment{}) add?
notes.back: A watch on the secondary type that follows each object's controller OwnerReference and enqueues its owner.

notes.front: When do you need Builder.Watches() with a mapping function instead of Owns()?
notes.back: When the relationship isn't an OwnerReference, e.g. a ConfigMap referenced by name. You supply handler.EnqueueRequestsFromMapFunc, usually backed by a field index, to map the changed object to primary keys.

notes.front: What is a controller-runtime Predicate?
notes.back: A filter on watch events deciding whether to enqueue. E.g. GenerationChangedPredicate ignores status- and metadata-only updates.

notes.front: What does returning ctrl.Result{RequeueAfter: d}, nil from Reconcile do?
notes.back: Schedules another reconcile after d without counting as a failure; for polling external state or waiting out a known condition.
notes.extra: Requeue: true requeues immediately through the rate limiter; newer controller-runtime versions deprecate it in favour of RequeueAfter.

notes.front: What should a Reconciler return on a transient error?
notes.back: The error. controller-runtime logs it and requeues the key with per-item exponential backoff; no manual RequeueAfter needed.

notes.front: How does controller-runtime avoid hot-looping on an object that keeps failing?
notes.back: The workqueue's per-item exponential backoff: each failure lengthens the delay up to a cap; success resets it (Forget).
notes.extra: It also stops a downed external API from being hammered at a fixed rate.

notes.front: What is a controller-runtime field indexer for?
notes.back: Indexing cached objects by a derived value so you can List by it without scanning: mgr.GetFieldIndexer().IndexField(ctx, &corev1.Pod{}, "spec.nodeName", fn), then client.MatchingFields{...}.

notes.front: What does SetupWithManager conventionally do?
notes.back: Builds the controller with ctrl.NewControllerManagedBy(mgr): For/Owns/Watches, predicates, options. Then registers it to start with the Manager.

notes.front: Why keep reconcile decision logic out of the Reconcile method's API plumbing?
notes.back: A pure function (observed state, desired state) to actions can be unit-tested with plain structs: no fake client, envtest or API server. Reconcile becomes thin glue.

notes.front: How is a finalizer handled in controller-runtime code?
notes.back: If obj.GetDeletionTimestamp().IsZero(), ensure controllerutil.AddFinalizer; otherwise run cleanup, then controllerutil.RemoveFinalizer and Update so deletion completes.

notes.front: Which controller-runtime helper marks a child object as owned by your CR?
notes.back: controllerutil.SetControllerReference(owner, child, scheme): sets an OwnerReference with controller: true, enabling garbage collection and Owns() routing.

notes.front: What breaks if the child objects of a custom resource (CR) are created without an OwnerReference to it?
notes.back: Deleting the CR leaves the children orphaned (no cascading garbage collection), and Owns() cannot route child events back to the CR. Also, an owner must be in the same namespace as its dependents (or be cluster-scoped).

notes.front: Why shouldn't an operator delete and recreate child objects on every reconcile?
notes.back: Churn: new UIDs, lost history, cascading deletes of grandchildren, brief outages, races with the garbage collector. Fetch, compare, and update only when different.
notes.extra: Helper: controllerutil.CreateOrUpdate (or CreateOrPatch) mutates the fetched object and writes only if it changed.

notes.front: A Kubernetes controller must be level-triggered. What does that mean for Reconcile, and why can't it rely on the event that triggered it?
notes.back: It computes what to do from the current observed state versus the desired state, not from which event fired. Events can be missed, coalesced by the workqueue, or replayed after a resync, and Reconcile receives only a namespace/name.

notes.front: What breaks if a Reconcile function is not idempotent?
notes.back: It is invoked repeatedly for the same object (retries after errors, resyncs, operator restarts, duplicate events), so non-idempotent steps such as blind Create calls cause duplicates or AlreadyExists errors. Make each pass check-then-act.

notes.front: Trace how a change in etcd ends up in your Reconcile call. List every hop.
notes.back: API server watch stream, informer reflector, local cache (store) updated, event handler, enqueue the namespace/name key, workqueue (deduplicates, rate-limits), a worker dequeues, Reconcile(ctx, req) reads the latest object from the cache.

notes.front: A controller creates a child object, then immediately reads it back with the default cached client and gets NotFound. Why, and how do you cope?
notes.back: The cache is fed by a watch and is eventually consistent, so it lags behind your own write. Tolerate NotFound (requeue and look again), or read through mgr.GetAPIReader() when a fresh read is required.

notes.front: How do you safely modify an object that you got from an informer cache or Lister?
notes.back: Call DeepCopy() first and modify the copy, then Update or Patch. The cached object is shared by every consumer, so mutating it in place corrupts the cache for all of them.

notes.front: Why can r.Update(ctx, obj) fail with a 409 Conflict, and how should a controller respond?
notes.back: Updates use optimistic concurrency: the resourceVersion on your copy is stale because someone else wrote first. Return the error so the key is requeued and reconciled from fresh state (or use Patch, or retry.RetryOnConflict).

notes.front: What breaks if a controller adds a finalizer to a custom resource (CR) but its cleanup path never removes it?
notes.back: The CR gets a deletionTimestamp but is never actually removed: it stays in Terminating forever, and its namespace cannot finish deleting either.

notes.front: Why should Reconcile not sleep or block while waiting for a Deployment to become ready, and what should it do instead?
notes.back: A blocked call occupies one of the few workers (MaxConcurrentReconciles defaults to 1), stalling every other object. Return promptly and let the Owns() watch or RequeueAfter trigger the next pass.

notes.front: A controller updates its own custom resource's status on every pass and watches that resource. What reconcile storm can result, and how do you stop it?
notes.back: Each status write is itself an update event that enqueues another reconcile. Use GenerationChangedPredicate (status writes do not bump metadata.generation) and avoid writing when nothing changed.

notes.front: Why write CR status with r.Status().Update()/Patch() rather than r.Update()?
notes.back: With the status subresource enabled, the main endpoint ignores status changes; Status() targets /status and avoids clobbering concurrent spec edits.

notes.front: What is status.observedGeneration for?
notes.back: The controller records the metadata.generation (spec version) it last processed. If it differs from the current generation, the reported status is stale because the controller has not yet acted on the latest spec.

notes.front: Mutating vs validating admission webhook (controller-runtime webhook package)?
notes.back: Mutating can change the object (e.g. defaults) before it is stored; validating can only accept or reject. Mutating webhooks run first.

notes.front: What is Kubebuilder in relation to controller-runtime?
notes.back: A scaffolding CLI on top of controller-runtime: generates the project layout, API types, controllers and Kustomize config, and uses markers so CRD and RBAC YAML are generated, not hand-written.

notes.front: What turns Kubebuilder markers into CRD YAML, RBAC and DeepCopy code, and when does it run?
notes.back: controller-gen, via make manifests and make generate. It is not part of go build, so rerun and commit after changing API types.

notes.front: What does the marker +kubebuilder:object:root=true do?
notes.back: Marks the type as a top-level Kind so controller-gen generates DeepCopyObject(), making it a runtime.Object.

notes.front: What do +kubebuilder:validation:... markers (e.g. Minimum=1, Enum=A;B) produce?
notes.back: OpenAPI v3 schema rules in the generated CRD, enforced by the API server on create/update, before your controller ever sees the object.

notes.front: What does a +kubebuilder:rbac:groups=...,resources=...,verbs=... marker generate?
notes.back: Rules in the operator's generated ClusterRole, aggregated across the code, keeping permissions next to the code that needs them.

notes.front: What does +kubebuilder:subresource:status do?
notes.back: Enables the /status subresource on the CRD: spec and status are written through separate endpoints and RBAC verbs, so a user's spec update can't overwrite controller-written status.
notes.analogy: Spec is the order form the customer fills in; status is the tracking page only the shop updates.

notes.front: What does +kubebuilder:printcolumn control?
notes.back: Extra columns in kubectl get for the CRD, e.g. Phase or Ready from status.

notes.front: When a Kubebuilder API has several versions, which marker picks the version stored in etcd?
notes.back: +kubebuilder:storageversion on exactly one version's type; other served versions are converted (conversion webhook / hub-and-spoke).

notes.text: Kubebuilder layout: Go API types live in {{c1::api/<version>/}}; reconcilers in {{c2::internal/controller/}}; Kustomize manifests (CRDs, RBAC, manager) in {{c3::config/}}.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::10 Operator Testing & Observability
notes.front: What is controller-runtime's envtest?
notes.back: A harness that starts real kube-apiserver and etcd binaries locally (no kubelet, scheduler or containers) so controller tests run against a genuine API server.
notes.analogy: A flight simulator with a real cockpit and instruments (API server) but no engines or runway (kubelet, scheduler).

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::10 Operator Testing & Observability
notes.front: Why prefer envtest over a fake client for reconcile tests, despite being slower?
notes.back: The real API server applies CRD schema validation, defaulting, admission and real Conflict/NotFound semantics, catching bugs a simplified fake would hide.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::10 Operator Testing & Observability
notes.front: What is the client-go fake clientset good for, and what doesn't it simulate?
notes.back: Fast in-memory unit tests of Get/List/Create logic. It skips validation, defaulting, admission webhooks and most server behaviour, so tests can pass that would fail on a cluster.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::10 Operator Testing & Observability
notes.front: envtest vs a kind cluster for operator tests?
notes.back: envtest: API server only; tests reconcile logic, nothing runs Pods. kind: a full cluster in Docker; e2e tests of the deployed image, RBAC, scheduling, networking.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::10 Operator Testing & Observability
notes.front: Why is Ginkgo/Gomega so common in operator projects?
notes.back: Kubebuilder scaffolds envtest suites with it, and Gomega's Eventually/Consistently fit asynchronous, eventually consistent reconcile behaviour.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::10 Operator Testing & Observability
notes.front: Why assert reconcile outcomes with Gomega Eventually(...) rather than after a time.Sleep?
notes.back: Reconcile is asynchronous and may take several passes. Eventually polls until a timeout: fast when things are quick, tolerant under slow CI. Fixed sleeps are flaky or slow.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::10 Operator Testing & Observability
notes.front: What does testing an admission webhook with envtest require?
notes.back: envtest can generate certs and register the webhook configurations, but your webhook server must be running and reachable for the test API server to call it.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::10 Operator Testing & Observability
notes.front: What is logr, and why does controller-runtime depend on it rather than a concrete logger?
notes.back: A minimal structured-logging interface (Info, Error, V(n), WithValues). The backend (zap, klog, slog) is pluggable without touching library code.
notes.analogy: logr is a standard wall socket; zap, klog or slog are the power plants behind it.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::10 Operator Testing & Observability
notes.front: Code in a Kubernetes operator logs through logr. Where does klog fit, and why can the output backend change without touching that code?
notes.back: logr is only an interface; klog/v2 can be one backend (or accept a logr sink), as can zap. Code written against logr is unaffected by which backend is chosen.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::10 Operator Testing & Observability
notes.front: Why use log.WithValues("namespace", ns, "name", n) in reconcilers instead of formatted strings?
notes.back: Key-value fields are machine-parseable by log pipelines and attach the same context to every later line of that reconcile.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::10 Operator Testing & Observability
notes.front: Why do logr/klog use verbosity levels V(n) instead of one debug flag?
notes.back: Detail can be dialled per process at runtime (V(0) normal, V(4)+ tracing) without rebuilding, and subsystems can log at different granularity.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::10 Operator Testing & Observability
notes.front: Which metrics does controller-runtime expose without extra code?
notes.back: Prometheus metrics per controller: reconcile totals, errors and duration, plus workqueue depth, latency and retries.

notes.deck: Go & Kubernetes Operators::10 Operator Testing & Observability
notes.front: What is an EventRecorder for, beyond logging?
notes.back: Emits Kubernetes Event objects attached to a specific resource (kubectl describe), giving users per-object history of what the controller did or why it failed.
notes.analogy: Events are notes stapled to the object's file; logs are the controller's private diary.
